title: WARD v. THE UNITED KINGDOM
summary:
In Ward v. the United Kingdom, the applicant, Mr. Martin Ward, is an Irish national and a member of the Traveller community, living with his family in a caravan on the Westway Travellers’ Site in London. Mr. Ward’s case highlighted the vulnerability of Roma and Traveller groups who are often forced to reside in substandard and hazardous environments due to a lack of suitable accommodation options. Since 1972, Mr. Ward and his family lived on a site situated directly beneath motorway flyovers and adjacent to a railway, exposing them to persistent noise and air pollution. Environmental health reports in 1992 and 2002 confirmed that the site was unsuitable for residential use, citing high nitrogen dioxide levels and intrusive noise, yet the local authority did not relocate the residents, opting instead for site refurbishment.

Mr. Ward argued that these living conditions, and the authorities’ failure to relocate the site, violated his rights under Article 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment) and Article 8 (right to respect for private and family life) of the European Convention on Human Rights. The European Court of Human Rights found the application inadmissible, concluding that the harm did not reach the severity required under Article 3, and that Article 8 was not violated, as the applicant had voluntarily chosen to remain on the site and had not demonstrated a lack of alternatives.

This case is significant as it underscores the persistent challenges faced by Roma and Traveller communities in securing safe and adequate housing, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in Europe, even as legal protections have evolved since the late twentieth century.
